edits.old: When $X$ is K\"ahler, the closed positive perturbations are cofinal among all Hermitian perturbations: a small positive multiple of one fixed K\"ahler form is below any given Hermitian form. edits.old: The complete metric supplied by Gauduchon traces describes normalized potentials with their $L^1$ topology. The ideal-envelope metric describes multiplier-ideal classes through their canonical representatives. Both are available without bounded mass. Neither gives the desired analogue of the source singularity geometry. The dyadic-envelope criterion of \cref{cor:dyadic-goodness-criterion} now characterizes $P_\theta[u]=Q_\theta[u]$ along a specified analytic regularization, without BMP. It does not define convergence for arbitrary ordinary singularity types; analytic classes are dense in the entire elementary ideal metric by \cref{cor:fixed-hermitian-analytic-density}.
edits.new: The complete metric supplied by Gauduchon traces describes normalized potentials with their $L^1$ topology. The ideal-envelope metric describes multiplier-ideal classes through their canonical representatives. Both are available without bounded mass. Neither gives the desired analogue of the source singularity geometry. The dyadic-envelope criterion of \cref{cor:dyadic-goodness-criterion} now characterizes $P_\theta[u]=P_\theta[u]_{\mathcal I}$ along a specified analytic regularization, without BMP. It does not define convergence for arbitrary ordinary singularity types; analytic classes are dense in the entire elementary ideal metric by \cref{cor:fixed-hermitian-analytic-density}.

edits.old: Construct a specified convergence for singularity types on an arbitrary Hermitian manifold that characterizes $P_\omega[u]=Q_\omega[u]$ by approximation with analytic singularities. edits.old: To see incompleteness concretely, choose a nonconstant smooth real function $f$. For sufficiently small $\varepsilon>0$, $\theta+\varepsilon\ddc f>0$. Put $u=\varepsilon f-\sup_Y(\varepsilon f)$. It is smooth, normalized and nonconstant. Its multiplier ideals are all trivial, so $Q_\theta[u]=0$, because zero is an admissible competitor. In particular $u\notin\mathfrak M_{\mathcal I}(Y,\theta)$. The preceding approximants $q_j$ are ideal envelopes, and their classes are Cauchy for $d_{\mathcal I,\theta,\mathrm{d}V}$ because $q_j\to u$ in $L^1$. If they converged in that metric to an ideal class, its envelope would agree almost everywhere, and hence everywhere, with $u$. This contradicts $Q_\theta[u]\ne u$.

edits.old: This example also proves that $Q_\theta$ is not continuous for $L^1$ on the normalized potentials: $Q_\theta[q_j]=q_j\to u$, but $Q_\theta[u]=0$. Compactifying the ideal classes by this elementary metric adds all normalized potentials on the curve. Those new points cannot be identified merely by their multiplier ideals, since many distinct smooth potentials have the same trivial ideals. A Hermitian singularity theory must specify whether it seeks such a compactification, a topology restricted by positive mass, or a different completion retaining additional data.
